responseSet.title: Walk in Clinics for Adolescents
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Walk in Clinics for Adolescents11

Jack Vick PHD

Jack Vick

Jack Vick   Brent Consultation Centre2

It is almost ten years since the Brent Consultation Centre started as a walk-in service for young people. The Centre has grown from its original small band of volunteers who were viewed with suspicion, to an organisation that is known both nationally and internationally for the quality of its work with adolescents. The extensive community work undertaken by members of the staff has resulted in increasing numbers of adolescents’ coming for help and the Education Department of the Borough of Brent has put the service on a sound and secure financial footing. Although the Centre has grown in size, now occupying a whole building, and has extended its service and increased its staff, the basic tenets of walk-in work have been maintained. This service is designed to meet the needs of adolescents and not the convenience of those who have to deal with them. The service is free, confidential and staffed by professionals with experience in work with adolescents. Access to these professional workers is made as easy as possible for the adolescent. There are no waiting lists, no referral is necessary and the adolescent need only walk in or telephone to be seen immediately.

Walk-in work has not only become an accepted form of reaching out to and dealing with the adolescent, but has in fact become one of the new fads. Walk-in and advice centres seem to be springing up every day. It is important therefore to examine the assumptions underlying the establishment of walk-in services, and the staffing requirements. We should look too at the limitations and possibilities within walk-in services and their potential for further development.

Looking back over the history of the Brent Consultation Centre and listening to those who ask for advice about starting or running a walk-in service, it has become apparent to me that there is an implicit assumption regarding the target population. It is assumed that there is a group of adolescents who, though troubled and unhappy, do not fall into the category of disturbed adolescents. These troubled but still “normal” adolescents should benefit from the support, advice and sympathetic ear of an older person. Such contact should be sufficient to set the adolescent on the right path and prevent more serious psychological breakdown. The supposition is that adolescents can be arrayed along a continuum from normal to pathological and walk-in services are then aimed at that large group in the middle of the continuum.

Living under the Threat of Death11

The Impact of a Congenital Illness on An Eight-Year-Old Boy

Juliet Hopkins

Juliet Hopkins

Juliet Hopkins  

Introduction

This paper is about a child's concern with life and death.

I present clinical material from the psychotherapy of Adam, a boy of eight years, whose first five years had been severely affected by a debilitating congenital illness which endangered his life. He required repeated treatment in hospital and his parents were told that he might not survive. Between the ages of five and eight years his health gradually improved, but the medical prognosis was that he would probably die before adulthood.

I briefly outline Adam's referral to our clinic and his history and family background, before I describe his expectations and anxieties as I encountered them in the early months of treatment. I then bring material which focuses on Adam's concern with the preservation and resuscitation of life and the evasion of death.

Referral and History

Adam was referred to our clinic at the age of eight years four months because he was failing at school. He was the first child of successful Jewish parents; his father was a writer and his mother a potter. He was born after a pregnancy fraught with anxiety on account of three prior miscarriages. At birth he was severely jaundiced and required a complete exchange transfusion. After a week in an incubator he returned to his mother who managed to breastfeed him until he was twelve weeks old, although his sucking made her nipples sore. He gained weight but was very pale and lacking in energy. Further investigations revealed him to be the victim of a severe anaemia, associated with mild jaundice, and caused by an enzyme deficiency. Treatment was by drugs, supplemented from the age of nine months by regular blood transfusions, at first needed every five months but increasing in frequency until by the age of four years they were given at two monthly intervals. [[RunningHead]]

A Psychoanalytically-Based Therapy as the Treatment of Choice for a Six-Year-Old Elective Mute11

Patricia Radford

Patricia Radford

Patricia Radford  

Part I. Introduction

I am going to attempt to illustrate the method of psychotherapy which I use in treating the emotionally ill children referred to me in a hospital setting. There are many controversies about the application of psychoanalytic principles and technique to, psychotherapy. These range between the ideas of Alexander (1954) that psychotherapy should be primarily uncovering, interpretative and insight-aiming, and the ideas of Bibring (1954) which indicate that dynamic psychotherapy is built around different selections or combinations of five major therapeutic techniques: suggestion, manipulation, abreaction, clarification and interpretation.

Tarachow (1963) considered that psychotherapy was basically a selective limited treatment in which rearrangement rather than resolution was the aim. Transference, repression and resistances are dealt with in such a way as to preserve their stability. Interestingly Malan (1967) described how when a group of psychoanalytically orientated psychotherapists embarked on a project to try to discover the limitation* of brief psychotherapy, they were surprised to find that their treatment bore the best results when there was a willingness on the part of the patient and the therapist to become deeply involved in depth and to bear the tension which ensued. In this type of psychotherapy involvement manifested itself in the transference experiences, the positive and negative aspects of which were interpreted and reconstructed in terms of early life experiences with the parental objects.

Most writers consider that the psychotherapist is more selective in his approach to the patient's material than is the psychoanalyst. Balint's (1972) group had a specific aim of working through a given aspect of psychopathology in a limited period. Tarachow (1963) assumed that the psychotherapist would disturb defences only in so far as was necessary to achieve the maximum therapeutic gain. It was, however, questioned how far psychotherapy could bring about the resolution of a derivative psychic conflict without the resolution of the basic conflict.

[[RunningHead]]

Stages towards the Containment of Mental Experience Illustrated in the Treatment of a Young Girl with Asthma11

Judith Elkan

Judith Elkan

Judith Elkan  

Introduction

The thoughts I am presenting in this paper are derived from my experience with an asthmatic girl who has been in once-weekly psychotherapy over a period of six years.

Jane was referred at the age of seven-and-a-half by the Paediatric Department of a children's hospital. At fourteen, she is now a tall, slender girl with a pleasing appearance and manner. She is the eldest in a family of two girls and two boys. There are close links with grandparents and many aunts and uncles.

The asthma commenced when Jane was two-and-a-half and coincided with the birth of a baby sister. The condition grew worse when, at four, Jane was sent with her sister to grandparents with whom she stayed for eight months. The parents were making plans to emigrate, though these did not materialise. Sometimes the asthmatic attacks were acute, and Jane had consultations at a number of hospitals. She had frequent attacks at night and about four wheezy mornings a week. Eventually she was referred for psychiatric investigation.

Jane was taken on for once-weekly therapy by a psychiatrist, and transferred to me after five months when the psychiatrist left the department. During the six years of therapy there have been two lengthy breaks, one of a year (when I had a baby) and one of two-and-a-half months. In addition to her psychotherapy, Jane has been prescribed Intal capsules used with an inhaler; these are meant to be used prophylactically three times a day.

Jane's birth was normal. On the second day her mother developed cystitis and had to be nursed in isolation. She fed Jane for three weeks only, as the milk ceased. Jane was toilet-trained by father by the age of one. When she was eighteen months, mother miscarried and was in hospital for five weeks. Jane was looked after at this time by the maternal grandmother and a maternal aunt who lived with Jane's parents. Another brief separation from mother came at two-and-a-half with the birth of the next baby. Jane was said not to have shown jealousy of the baby, though mother had been expecting it. However, when the baby was named Annette, Jane wanted her own name to be changed to Janet.

responseSet.title: The Abuse of Psychiatry for Political Purposes
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Abuse of Psychiatry for Political Purposes

Elizabeth Holder

Elizabeth Holder

Elizabeth Holder  

Most people are aware of at least some of the facts of psychiatric abuse in the U S S.R. and Eastern Europe. In recent conversations about professional ethics and the question of an individual's and society's responsibility for upholding moral codes of practice and condemning immoral ones, I have been asked “What can we do?” I have been told that the majority of child analysts are not psychiatrists, from which I am to infer that it is none of our business; or the word “politics” has been muttered darkly and our blessed neutrality invoked to calm any quiverings of the super ego.

I think such reactions must arise from the need in most of us to develop some kind of defensive armour against the battery of atrocities and inhumanities forced upon us daily. We feel hopeless in face of them all and turn to our own bit of humanitarian work, where the same ethic applies whether we are psychiatrists, psychoanalysts, social workers, or members of the medical profession. If this basic humanitarian ethic is being systematically violated by a core of Russian psychiatrists, why should we react?

The reason is historical and inescapable. In 1931 a group of Bavarian psychiatrists discussed openly the principles and needs for sterilisation and euthanasia. By 1936, extermination of the “physically or socially unfit” was accepted practice.

All state mental hospitals and homes for retarded children had to report on patients who had been ill for over five years. The decision as to which patients should be killed was carried out by consultants, most of whom were professors of psychiatry. They never saw the patients.

Those first exterminations of human beings for political reasons were carried out by medical men under the guise of sickness. The killings went from the mentally retarded, the “chronic schizophrenic”, “the criminally insane” to the “racially impure”.

Thus medical anti-humanism begins with very simple shifts of attitude in the doctors involved. All that was necessary in Germany was to show that life is not worthy to be lived in certain circumstances. A similar effective shift has been made by Russian psychiatrists against the dissenter, in creating a form of political diagnosis indicating that these people are “useless and incurably sick” in terms of the society in which they live. So once again medical men are being used to circumvent the law, and the political system sanctions the new ethic and assimilates it into a new moral code. Already psychiatric diagnosis has been changed to fit a political system, and it is a simple move from political dissenters to religious deviates, human rights activists, nationalists mainly from the Ukraine and Lithuania, and would-be emigrants.

[[RunningHead]]

Problems of Dependence and Development: Discussion

Charlotte Riley

Charlotte Riley

Charlotte Riley  

I would like to thank Mrs. Alvarez for her very interesting paper which brings together in a lively, descriptive way some of the central developments in this treatment, which must have often felt long and laborious, despite considerable progress. She has given us a most valuable description of Bobbie's method of psychic survival through sticking to his object, and of the analytic struggle toward recognising the separateness and aliveness of himself and his object.

Of the many aspects of this case which might be discussed, I would like to focus on an impression I had of the insistent way in which Bobbie created and lived in an exclusive, two-object world. Certainly, he tried to overcome the separateness implicit in even the two-person relationship, but from his first session he knew that what he was needing was a bridge. What particularly struck me was the relative absence of direct material concerning jealousy and rivalry, especially as compared with material from other autistic children who often seem preoccupied with these problems at however primitive a level. It seemed to me that Bobbie was involved in an evasion of the third object in his relation to his internal mother, along with the attendant pain and anxiety which are so much a part of establishing any separate identity and allowing one's object and one's internal world to come to life. This third object to be avoided would be felt at different developmental levels as the intruding hardness of the nipple in the child's relation to the soft breast, as the father, or as the other babies felt to be coming between him and the mother.

The intensity and exclusiveness of Bobbie's relationship to his therapist which came across to me as part of the ambience of his analysis is probably connected to the urgency of attention Mrs. Alvarez felt Bobbie to evoke from her, as well as his mode of sticking himself to his object. His collapses and his enormous difficulty in internalising an object with any firmness, grasp or capacity for thought derive from his adhesion to his object, but also from his non-recognition of the firm internal father within his maternal object. Perhaps a delicate balance exists here as to when interpretations of this problem would be premature intrusions into the child's attempts to become established with his primary maternal object, and when the evasion of his jealousy and rivalry are central to his difficulties in object relations. These issues are integral to the technical problems Mrs. Alvarez has called “just how soft to make it” for Bobbie.

responseSet.title: La Faim Et Le Corps by Evelyne Kestemberg, Jean Kestemberg, Simone Decobert Published by Presses Universitaires de France
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

La Faim Et Le Corps by Evelyne Kestemberg, Jean Kestemberg, Simone Decobert Published by Presses Universitaires de France

Kate Paul

Kate Paul

Kate Paul  

Although “La Faim Et Le Corps” (“Hunger and the Body”) was published as long ago as 1972, our attention can still usefully be drawn to this work of some of our colleagues in France. Dr. and Mme. Kestemberg and Mme. Decobert have presented an explorative and moving account of psychotherapy and psychodrama with anorexic adolescents.

Reading the book, one lives through some of the authors’ discoveries and some of their anxieties and bewilderments. The book itself is a kind of journey. The writing is lively and especially apt and vivid when clinical material is described and where the typical anorexic is characterised. “There is a secret megalomania constantly agitating in the shadow of a pitiable, neglected body, whose pleasure is concentrated in the speechless drunkenness of hunger, sought and found and ramified in the vertigo of domination of the beast by his rider; anyone who through their maladroit attention thinks that they speak to the rider, the cavalier, is heard as only being interested in the beast”.

As is well known, anorexia commonly appears in adolescence when sexual development would normally bring into focus the parental relationship. It appears that the anorexic cannot tolerate an awareness of the Parents' sexual identities and sexual relationship. This implies separateness and lack of omnipotent control on the part of the adolescent, who until now has lived on a false basis. Winnicott is referred to here. Compliance, comparative success, hidden stubborness which can pass for strength, have been the child's way of concealing a strongly fused relationship with mother, involving projective identification. This fusion is thought to be caused by a peculiarity in the infantile relationship with the mother, who was unable to experience her child except as a part of herself. Hence both control and physical contact would be experienced by the infant as unsafe; he would experience the mother as all too easily entered, excited and controlled.

The mother's “narcissistic” relation to her child as a part of herself and of her own body is at first linked by the authors to castration anxiety and the oedipus complex. Only later in the book is the anxiety described as being on a pre-oedipal level. The use of oedipal concepts is found to be inaccurate insofar as the fused identity of the anorexic does not allow the development of a view of the parents as separate, of male and female as different. The oedipal situation is thus denied and retreated from. The inadequacy of classical language and concepts to describe anorexia seems to have been borne in on the authors during the writing of this book.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Psychotherapy of an Adolescent Case of Anorexia Nervosa11

Giuliana Fortunato and Donald Meltzer

Donald Meltzer

Donald Meltzer  

Introduction

The treatment of Luigi covered the four years from the age of fourteen, during which time he was never seen more than once a week. I had the opportunity of hearing about it on five occasions during the latter half of the therapy, and found the progress so impressive and the material so interesting that I asked Mrs. Fortunato to write it up with a view to publication. Despite the relative infrequency of the sessions a dynamic and deep-going transference developed and underwent extensive evolution. Although her technique relied mainly on observation and thought and relatively little on continuous interpretive activity, its power to assist the evolution of the transference is impressive. The fascinating way in which this evolution is paralleled by the metamorphosis of Luigi's social life, especially in his club, the Tabina, raises important questions about the limits of the concept of acting out. Finally the termination process shows with unusual clarity the interplay of dependence, relinquishment and the need for freedom in an adolescent patient.

Case Presentation

When Luigi first came to the Department of Child Psychiatry he was fourteen-and-a-half. Some months earlier his father had rather peremptorily demanded treatment for his son who had been suffering from the age of thirteen from a digestive disturbance, finally diagnosed as anorexia nervosa, after exhaustive examinations and drug therapies. For periods the boy had refused to eat for fear of “indigestion” and at other times ate in such a haphazard way that his weight had fallen as low as 29 kilos. Other symptoms included headaches, constipation and nausea.

Because of the emaciation a two months period in a nursing home was necessary before psychotherapy could be started on an out-patient basis, one session per week only being feasible. The nursing home, where some psycho-therapeutic effort had been made, along with feeding and transfusions, continued to follow Luigi's medical state.

The family situation was described in a history written by the father. In it he revealed himself as rigid, intrusive and dictatorial, posing as the ideal parent, but was clearly obsessive, conventional and lacking in emotion.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Self and AutismMichael Fordham Published by Heinemann

Jess Guthrie

Jess Guthrie

Jess Guthrie  

This important book makes a valuable and original contribution to analytical psychology in its understanding of children. It is well known that Jung in his investigations, clinical work and formulation of theory was mostly concerned with adults in the second half of life. His immediate followers gave so much importance to the effect of the Parents' unconscious conflicts on their children that no consistent body of knowledge concerning younger people was built up.

Fordham has for long realised that much that was given no definite statement was implied in Jung's work. He studied these implications closely in their original context, and has tested their validity over a long period of clinical work and observation of children. In the result, he has shown that the theories of the archetypes and the self can increase our understanding of maturation and development of the personality in infancy and through childhood and adolescence into adult life.

Jung introduced the theory of archetypes to account for the regularity of the images, often mythological, which occurred in the dreams and imagination of adults. As well as being felt to be important by the individuals who experienced them, they were reflected in religion and the organisations within society where they were found to constitute an important element in the psychology of groups. Thus the regularity of their recurrence showed a general and probably a universal distribution.

The archetypes are considered to be dynamic structures within the personality and closely related with the instincts, but differ from the ethologists’ release mechanisms in being bipolar. On the one hand they find expression in instinctive impulses and on the other in fantasy or spiritual form. The images through which the archetypes are represented in consciousness can be affected by education and upbringing and they change with maturation and life experience.

In order to establish how much this theory could have application also to the first stages of life, Fordham set out to discover how early in childhood the archetypal images occur. Being very familiar with the predominance of body imagery in infancy, he tested out his idea that the archetypes could find expression in neurophysical structures and biochemical changes. The results of this, together with his postulate that there is in childhood a predisposition to develop archaic feelings, ideas and fantasies, showed that the archetypes can be seen to bring body and psyche together. He comments on how the description some Kleinians give of unconscious phantasy comes close to Jung's definition of the archetype.

[[RunningHead]]

Living under the Threat of Death: Discussion

Anne Hurry

Anne Hurry

Anne Hurry  

I would like to thank Mrs. Hopkins for her extremely interesting paper. It was an especially appropriate one for the opening of our study weekend, because of the bridges it builds between the various theoretical points of view represented among us. I was particularly glad to see the use made of Marion Milner's thinking — her contribution being one we often neglect.

Clinically Mrs. Hopkins has given us a sensitive exposition of the impact upon a child of medical procedures, not only detailing the particular meanings which accrued to such experiences in this case, but also indicating the way in which interferences in the realms of narcissism and masochism may arise. She has shared with us a child's experience of gradually becoming safe enough with her to allow himself to become absorbed in transitional play, to take delight in it, and even to begin to accept disillusionment. I found this paper a fruitful and stimulating one, and there are many things we could discuss. I have restricted myself to four points.

Firstly, we should take note of the fact that this boy was not in full psychoanalysis, or even twice weekly treatment, but was seen only once a week. While I am sure Mrs. Hopkins must often have wished she could see him more often, and Adam himself made his wish clear in the fourth session, there is no doubt that the technique throughout was strictly psychoanalytic, that a transference was maintained from week to week, and that in only sixty-six sessions important changes took place in this child's inner world and in his behaviour. We often underestimate the work which can be done in once weekly sessions: both this paper and Miss Radford's study of once weekly treatment with an elective mute (Radford 1977), provide valuable evidence as to what can be achieved.

Secondly, I have some questions about the nature of Adam's relationship with his sister. I fully agree with Mrs. Hopkins that Adam used his sister as a vehicle for the externalisation of the unacceptable aspects of his self, such as his wishes to mess or his jealousy. But I question how far he was really employing the mechanism of altruistic surrender, and how far he was thereby enabled to avoid the fear of death. Anna Freud (1936) describes how in most altruistic patients the vehicle for externalisation has been the object of envy, and the altruistic surrender a method of overcoming narcissistic mortification. It seems to me that Adam's feelings of helplessness and mortification are still conscious, although we see him struggling to be in control, while his envy of his sister, both as a sibling and as the possessor of bounding health, is still at least pre-conscious.

Problems of Dependence and Development in an Excessively Passive Autistic Boy11

Anne Alvarez

Anne Alvarez

Anne Alvarez  

Introduction

My subject is a seventeen-year-old autistic boy whom I have been treating by the psycho-analytical method over a period of ten years. I will outline certain developments which have taken place in him during this period, but I should say from the start that these developments are limited. They are limited both by the nature of his illness, which seems designed to prevent innovation and change, and also by the considerable interruptions to which his treatment was exposed in his first six years at the Clinic.

I hope to show how he began his treatment with an effort at making contact with me as a way of overcoming intolerable anxieties about separation and separateness; how, to a large extent, he lost this link during the early interrupted years, and how he gradually came to find it again. I would also like to say something about two very different methods he now employs for achieving this contact. One of these seems to promote change and growth and life in him, while the other is death to development.

Referral

Bobbie was referred to a consultant in 1963 at age four with a note from his G.P. that he was backward in speech and behaviour, and at times very withdrawn. He was psychologically tested then and several times since, and is estimated to be of at least average intelligence. Five times weekly treatment was recommended, but the parents could not manage it, and Bobbie started at the Clinic twice weekly with his first therapist late in 1963. His mother was seen by a case worker, and they met most of the time in a foursome.

Bobbie spoke little, used to walk into ponds, run into the road, and would try desperately to stick fallen leaves back on to trees. He never used the word “I” and once in nursery school said that a jigsaw was a “broken mummy”. I used to see him on the stairs of the Clinic and he was an appealing, delicate looking child with a lost, floppy, rag-doll look about him.

History

Bobbie's parents, together with the maternal grandparents, came here from abroad a year before he was born.

“My Ambition is to Be Dead” The Analysis of Motives and Reasons for Suicide Behaviour in an Adolescent Girl, with Particular Reference to the Relationship between the Adolescent Process and Suicide

Part I: Case Study1

Anne Hurry

Anne Hurry

Anne Hurry  

Introduction

Suicide is a major cause of death among young people in industrialised countries, often superceded only by death through accident or cancer (Haim, 1969). In addition there are large numbers of young people who attempt suicide: estimates vary from eight to fifty times as many as succeed (Stengel, 1964; Haim, 1969). Yet child suicide, while it does occur, is very rare.

We have still to clarify what it is about the adolescent process that makes suicide possible. Psychiatric literature is of little help, being divided as to the degree and type illness involved in adolescent suicide (e.g. Barraclough et. al., 1974; Balser and Masterson, 1959; White, 1974).

Psychoanalytic literature provides more clarification than is at first evident. Suicide has been a subject of analytic study from the publication of “The Psychopathology of Everyday Life” (Freud, 1901) onwards, but it is not generally recognised that many of the early case histories are about adolescents, and that much of the early theorising sprang from work with young people: the 1910 Symposium of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society (Ed. Friedman, 1967) was related to suicide among students aged between 15 and 20. And recently there have been a number of contributions specifically related to adolescence (Friedman et. al., 1972; Haim, 1969, Havens, 1969; Kernberg, 1974; Schneer and Kay, 1961; Schneer, 1974; Stone, 1973). But each new contribution tends to emphasise one aspect at the expense of others, with the notable exception of Haim (1969) who, unfortunately, does not include clinical material. And Pauline Kernberg, in “The analysis of a fifteen-and-a-half-year old with suicidal tendencies” (1974) comments upon how many of the dynamic factors described in the literature were to be found in her case, but does not attempt to classify
